newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-ITALY'S TOUGH ON FOREIGN COACHES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ITALY'S TOUGH ON FOREIGN COACHES.

text.p: The sacking of Roma's Argentine coach Carlos Bianchi last week again underlines the difficulties encountered by non-Italian coaches in Italy's ultra-competitive serie A.
Five of the six serie A coaches replaced since the beginning of the season have been foreigners and Bianchi suggests the Italian soccer environment is less tolerant of foreign than native coaches.

The other foreigners to feel the axe this season are Uruguayan Gregorio Perez of Cagliari, Romanian Mircea Lucescu of Reggiana and Czech Zdenek Zeman of Lazio while Perez's compatriot Oscar Washington Tabarez of AC Milan resigned.

In an interview in this week's French soccer magazine "France Football", Bianci said: "They use different standards for different people...For example, Carlo Ancelotti is currently being lauded for having success with a Parma side that has been successful for a number of seasons and contains eight international players.

"In contrast, people are very critical of (Englishman) Roy Hodgson who, according to them, has been a failure at Inter even though the team have one foot in the UEFA Cup final, are third in the league and were knocked out of the Italian Cup only in a semifinal penalty shoot-out..."
With seven games still to play in serie A, Parma are currently second on 49 points, three behind leaders Juventus and four in front of Internazionale.

Bianchi's reference to Hodgson is ironic since the Inter coach has already announced that he, too, will be leaving Italian soccer at the end of the season to take up the manager's job at English premier league side Blackburn.

Although Hodgson has not gone on record to explain his decision to leave Inter, sources close to the club suggest he has been dismayed by season-long criticism from Inter fans and sections of the Italian sports press.
Speaking on Monday to students at Milan's Cattolica University, Hodgson commented on his problems with fans and media alike.
"I must say I have to ask myself what has happened among our fans in recent weeks that they want to do this (whistle and jeer Hodgson) even when we are going well in two competitions.

"However, I don't need to read the papers to know whether or not my work is going well and the truth is that...in Italy you need only to lose two games to have years of good work demolished and it's equally true that with two good performances you are again being praised to the skies."
The jury is probably still out on the issue of foreign coaches in Italy.
What is sure, however, is that with the departure of Hodgson, there will be only one foreigner certain to coach in serie A next season -- Swede Sven Goran Eriksson.
At present coach to Sampdoria, Eriksson is due to move to Roman club Lazio at the end of the season.
Apart from Lazio, other serie A clubs looking for a new coach appear to be concentrating on finding experienced Italians.
Ailing champions AC Milan are reportedly looking into replacing Arrigo Sacchi with another former coach, Fabio Capello, at present with Spanish league leaders Real Madrid.
Inter will replace Hodgson with current Napoli coach Luigi Simoni, while Roma have made contact with Giovanni Trapattoni, now with German league leaders Bayern Munich.
Trapattoni, however, is believed to want to stay with Bayern.

One man apparently determined to swim against the tide is the 1978 World Cup winning coach, Argentine Cesar Menotti, at present with Argentine club side Independiente but reportedly negotiating a move to succeed Eriksson at Sampdoria.
Menotti will need all his vast experience and skill and considerable diplomacy if he is to survive for long in Italy.
